source.title: The Prophet
source.attribution: Kahlil Gibran, The Prophet, Standard Ebooks, public domain

cards.title: Close couples still need room to be themselves
cards.body:
Gibran's advice on marriage is to be together without fusing into one person. Share your lives, but let each partner keep their own interests, friends and quiet time, like two strings on the same instrument that each make their own sound.

Couples sometimes feel that wanting space means something is wrong. Often the opposite is true: people who keep growing as individuals bring more to the relationship. A solo hobby, a separate weekend with friends or an evening apart can strengthen the bond rather than weaken it.
cards.quote: But let there be spaces in your togetherness
cards.apply_it: Ask your partner (or reflect, if single) about one interest each of you would like more personal time for, and plan room for it.

quiz.question: What does Gibran recommend for a marriage?
quiz.explanation: He advises closeness with room for each person, like separate strings playing the same music.

cards.title: Your children are not copies of you
cards.body:
Gibran reminds parents that children come through them but don't belong to them. You can give them love, a home and guidance, but not your thoughts; they will grow into a future you can't fully see.

It is tempting to steer kids toward the career, hobbies or beliefs you wish you had. Gibran suggests the opposite: learn from them and let them become themselves. That might mean supporting a path you wouldn't pick, while still providing a stable base from which they can launch.
cards.quote: You may strive to be like them, but seek not to make them like you.
cards.apply_it: Ask a child (or younger person) in your life what they are excited about right now, and listen without steering.

quiz.question: What does Gibran advise parents about their children?
options: Give them your love but not your thoughts
quiz.explanation: Children have their own thoughts; parents can be like them but shouldn't try to make them copies.

cards.title: Work done with care feeds people; work done with indifference shortchanges them
cards.body:
Gibran's chapter on work ends with a striking claim: work is love made visible. Bread baked with indifference is bitter and only half satisfies.

In any job, people can feel whether you cared: the email that actually answers the question, the code with clear names, the meal made with attention. Care doesn't require loving every task. It means imagining the person who will use what you make and doing it as if they mattered, because they do. That attitude often turns routine work into something meaningful.
cards.quote: For if you bake bread with indifference, you bake a bitter bread that feeds but half man’s hunger.
cards.apply_it: Before your next routine task, picture the specific person who will use the result. Do one extra thing that would make it better for them.

quiz.question: What happens, in Gibran's image, when bread is baked with indifference?
options: It feeds only half of a person's hunger
quiz.explanation: Indifferent work falls short; Gibran calls work done with care 'love made visible'.

cards.title: Sorrow and joy grow from the same places in your life
cards.body:
Gibran writes that joy and sorrow are inseparable. What makes you happy, a person, a place, a calling, is exactly what can later make you grieve. And the deeper sorrow carves into you, the more joy you are able to hold.

This is a useful lens in hard times. Grief over a lost relationship or a pet shows how much they mattered. Painful experiences can also make you more sensitive to small pleasures afterwards. Allowing both feelings, instead of numbing one, keeps you able to feel the other.
cards.quote: The deeper that sorrow carves into your being, the more joy you can contain.
cards.apply_it: Think of something you have grieved. Write one sentence on what it shows you value, and one way you can honour that today.

quiz.question: What does Gibran say about the relationship between joy and sorrow?
options: Sorrow should be avoided at all costs
They are inseparable, coming from the same source
quiz.explanation: He sees them as two sides of the same well; sorrow can deepen our capacity for joy.

cards.title: Steer with reason, move with passion; you need both
cards.body:
Gibran compares reason and passion to the rudder and sails of a ship. Without sails, you go nowhere; without a rudder, you drift or crash. Reason alone confines, and passion without guidance burns itself out.

People often treat feelings and logic as enemies. In practice, good decisions use both: emotion tells you what you care about and gives energy, while reasoning chooses the route. Next time you're torn, ask what your feelings are telling you and what your judgement says, then look for a path that honours both.
cards.quote: For reason, ruling alone, is a force confining; and passion, unattended, is a flame that burns to its own destruction.
cards.apply_it: For one decision you're facing, write what your feelings want and what your reasoning says. Look for an option that respects both.

quiz.question: In Gibran's image, what are reason and passion?
options: The rudder and sails of a ship
quiz.explanation: Reason steers and passion propels; each fails without the other.

cards.title: Seek friends to share life with, not just to kill time
cards.body:
Gibran draws a distinction between seeing a friend with 'hours to kill' and with 'hours to live'. One treats friendship as filler for boredom; the other brings your real self and full attention.

It's easy to meet friends while half-scrolling, or only when there is nothing better to do. Gibran asks for more: give your friend your best, share your good tides and not only your low ones, and enjoy laughter and small pleasures together. Presence, not time spent, is what deepens a friendship.
cards.quote: For what is your friend that you should seek him with hours to kill?
cards.apply_it: Next time you meet a friend, put your phone away for the whole visit and share one good thing in your life, not just problems.

quiz.question: What does Gibran mean by seeking a friend with 'hours to live'?
options: Bringing real presence instead of using them to fill empty time
Spending as many hours as possible together
quiz.explanation: He contrasts filling idle time with truly living alongside a friend.

cards.title: Notice when you're talking only to avoid sitting with your thoughts
cards.body:
Gibran observes that we often talk when we are no longer at peace with our own thoughts. Some people seek out chatty company because silence would leave them face to face with themselves.

Today the same urge reaches for podcasts, calls or scrolling the moment a quiet minute appears. Constant noise can crowd out real thinking. Spending a little time in silence, on a walk or a commute without audio, lets thoughts settle and makes your later words more considered.
cards.quote: And in much of your talking, thinking is half murdered.
cards.apply_it: Take a ten-minute walk or commute today with no audio and no phone. Notice what thoughts come up.

quiz.question: According to Gibran, what often happens to thinking in much of our talking?
quiz.explanation: He suggests that constant talk can crowd out thought, often as a way to escape our own company.
